title: Pre-Construction Planning: Why It Matters More Than the Build
subtitle: A Keentel General Contractors Technical Publication

ctaText: Don't let your project discover problems during construction. Let's talk about pre-construction planning and how it protects your timeline, budget, and peace of mind.
content:
The project didn't go wrong during construction.

It went wrong six months earlier — in a meeting where someone said 'let's just get started and figure it out as we go.'

We've seen it dozens of times. An owner with a clear vision, a real budget, and a genuine need to build. A contractor eager to mobilize. And a pre-construction process that was compressed, skipped, or treated as a formality.

The result is always the same. The project discovers its problems during construction — the most expensive possible time to discover them.

Pre-construction planning is how you move those discoveries to before the build. Where changing a wall costs a conversation. Not a change order.

The decisions made before construction begins are responsible for 80% of what determines whether a project succeeds. Pre-construction is where that 80% happens.

Most Projects Fail Before Ground Breaks

This is not hyperbole. It's pattern recognition from 30+ years of construction in Florida.

When we examine projects that went significantly over budget, over schedule, or under quality expectations, the root causes almost never originate in the construction phase itself.

They originate in:

  • A scope that was never fully defined
  • A budget built on assumptions nobody tested
  • A schedule that didn't account for Florida's permitting timelines
  • A site investigation that wasn't done — or wasn't done properly
  • A design that looked right on paper but couldn't be built as drawn
  • Long-lead materials that nobody ordered until it was too late
  • Stakeholders who had different expectations and never reconciled them

Every one of these is a pre-construction failure. Every one of them is preventable.

The Hard Truth → A contractor who is eager to skip pre-construction and 'get started' is either inexperienced or prioritizing their cash flow over your project outcome. The fastest way to a troubled project is starting construction before the project is ready to be built.

What Pre-Construction Actually Is

Pre-construction is not paperwork. It's not a project kickoff meeting. It's not the week between signing the contract and breaking ground.

Pre-construction is the structured phase of work — typically 4 to 16 weeks depending on project complexity — that transforms a project idea into a buildable, financeable, schedulable plan.

Done properly, it's the most intensive strategic work on the project. And it's the work that makes the build feel almost easy by comparison.

What Pre-Construction Covers

PhaseWhat HappensWhy It Matters
1. DiscoveryProject goals, budget parameters, schedule requirements, operational constraints definedMisaligned expectations here cost more than any other mistake
2. Site EvaluationGeotechnical, environmental, utility, zoning, boundary assessmentUncovers the surprises before they're crises
3. Conceptual BudgetingCost models built from real scope, real site, real market dataGives you numbers you can actually plan around
4. Design CoordinationContractor works alongside architects and engineersConstructability reviewed before drawings are locked
5. Value EngineeringAlternative specs, materials, and methods evaluated for cost-quality trade-offsThe cheapest time to make design changes is on paper
6. Schedule DevelopmentCritical path built — procurement, permitting, construction, inspectionsLong-lead items ordered, permit timelines planned, no surprises
7. Procurement PlanningSubcontractors identified, long-lead materials sourcedPrevents the supply chain delays that stop construction cold
8. Construction ReadinessFinal drawings, permits, trade mobilization — project is ready to buildEverything in place before ground breaks

The Principle → Pre-construction converts unknowns into knowns. Every unknown that enters construction as a surprise costs more — in money, in time, and in relationships — than the same unknown discovered and resolved during planning.

The Cost of Change Curve — The Most Important Chart in Construction

There's a concept in construction project management called the Cost of Change Curve.

The idea is simple: the cost of making any given change to a project increases exponentially as the project advances.

Here's what that looks like in real numbers:

Project StageCost to Change $100K of ScopeReality
Pre-Design / Discovery$1,000 – $5,000A conversation and a few hours of design time
Schematic Design$5,000 – $20,000Rework early drawings — painful but manageable
Design Development$20,000 – $60,000Significant rework, consultant fees, schedule impact
Construction Documents$40,000 – $100,000Redesign, re-permit, full consultant revision cycle
During Construction$150,000 – $300,000+Stop work, demolish, rebuild — contractor change orders
After CompletionNot possible or $400,000+You live with it, or you pay for a full renovation

Read that table carefully.

A change that costs a conversation during pre-design costs $150,000 to $300,000+ if it's discovered during construction.

This is why pre-construction is not overhead. It's the highest-ROI investment in the project.

Pre-construction doesn't add cost to your project. It prevents costs from being added to your project.

The 6 Things Pre-Construction Protects You From

1. The Budget That Was Never Real

The most common pre-construction failure is budgeting without a proper scope.

An owner says 'we have $3 million.' A contractor says 'we can do that.' Nobody has actually verified whether $3 million can build what the owner envisions on the specific site they're considering, with the finish level they have in mind, in the current Florida labor market.

Pre-construction answers that question before it's too late to adjust.

Real budgeting requires real scope. Real scope requires site investigation, design development, and contractor cost input. Pre-construction is the process that produces all three.

2. The Site That Hid Its Problems

In 30+ years of building in Florida, we have learned to assume that every site has a story.

Sometimes it's a high water table that requires expensive dewatering and foundation modifications. Sometimes it's poor soil bearing capacity that wasn't visible on the surface. Sometimes it's underground utilities in the wrong place. Sometimes it's environmental contamination from a prior use.

None of these are dealbreakers. All of them are more expensive to address during construction than before it.

Pre-construction site investigation — geotechnical borings, environmental assessment, utility survey, boundary survey — surfaces these issues when the response is a design adjustment. Not a six-figure change order.

Florida Note → Florida's geology is particularly variable. High water tables are common across the peninsula. Karst geology — limestone that can develop sinkholes — exists across significant portions of Central and North Florida. Coastal sites carry additional regulatory requirements. A geotechnical investigation is not optional here. It's how you find out what you're building on.

3. The Design That Couldn't Be Built

Architects design for what should be. Contractors build what can be.

When designers and contractors work in isolation — which is the standard model in traditional construction — the gap between those two realities shows up as change orders.

Pre-construction brings the contractor into the design process early. Constructability reviews happen while design decisions are still fluid. The contractor flags the details that are expensive or impossible to execute as drawn — before the drawings are complete, before permits are applied for, before crews are on site.

This is the core value of integrated pre-construction. Not just planning. Collaboration between the people who design and the people who build, at the moment when collaboration is cheapest.

4. The Schedule That Was Never Achievable

'We need to be open by Q1.'

That's a goal. A schedule is built from actual tasks, actual durations, and actual dependencies — permit timelines, material lead times, inspection holds, subcontractor availability, and Florida's storm season.

Pre-construction produces a critical path schedule that accounts for all of these variables. It identifies the long-lead items — structural steel, custom MEP equipment, specialty finishes — that must be ordered before construction begins or they become the constraint that blows the schedule.

In Florida, where commercial permit timelines in high-volume municipalities can run 8–16 weeks, this planning is the difference between a project that opens on time and one that doesn't.

5. The Stakeholders Who Had Different Visions

This one is underestimated almost universally.

Every project has multiple stakeholders — owners, investors, lenders, future occupants, operations teams. They often have different assumptions about what's being built, at what cost, and to what standard.

Pre-construction is the structured process that surfaces and resolves those differences before they become disputes.

A scope document. A budget narrative. A design review. A schedule presentation. These are pre-construction deliverables. They're also the tools that ensure everyone who has a voice in the project is aligned before work begins.

6. The Change Order Cascade

Change orders are the most expensive thing in construction that most owners never anticipate.

Not because contractors are dishonest. Because projects that skipped proper pre-construction enter construction with gaps — in scope, in design, in site understanding — that must be resolved as they're discovered. And resolving them during construction is always more expensive than resolving them during planning.

Pre-construction doesn't eliminate change orders. Nothing does. But it reduces them dramatically — and ensures the ones that remain are genuine scope changes, not the predictable consequences of inadequate planning.

What Pre-Construction Looks Like in Practice at Keentel

We don't treat pre-construction as a checkbox before the real work starts.

It is the real work — for us and for our clients.

Here's what our pre-construction process delivers:

  • A project scope document that every stakeholder has reviewed and agreed to
  • A construction budget built from current Florida market data, your specific site, and your specific design — not industry averages
  • A constructability review of the design with specific flagged items and recommended modifications
  • A value engineering analysis identifying where budget can be saved without compromising function or quality
  • A critical path project schedule with permit timeline built in
  • A procurement plan with long-lead items identified and ordered
  • A risk register — the known unknowns documented and planned for
  • Construction readiness: permits applied for, subcontractors lined up, materials in motion

When our crews mobilize on day one of construction, the project is ready to be built. Not almost ready. Not we'll-figure-it-out-as-we-go ready. Ready.

The Keentel Standard → We will not mobilize for construction until pre-construction is complete. Not as a policy. Because we've seen what happens when projects skip it — and we're not willing to put our clients through that. Call 813-395-0000 or visit keentelgeneralcontractors.com to start the conversation.

When Should Pre-Construction Begin?

Earlier than you think.

The ideal time to engage a general contractor for pre-construction is during schematic design — when the project vision is clear but the design is still fluid.

At this stage:

  • Budget input can still influence design decisions
  • Site investigation findings can still shape the approach
  • Long-lead material procurement can begin before construction starts
  • Permit applications can be positioned for the earliest possible submission

Many owners wait until design is complete to engage a GC. By then, the most valuable pre-construction work — the work that shapes the design — is no longer possible. What remains is just pricing a set of drawings.

That's not pre-construction. That's bidding.

Engaging a contractor after design is complete is like hiring a navigator after you've already committed to the route. They can help. But they can't take you somewhere different.

Pre-Construction Is How Keentel Differentiates

There are a lot of general contractors in Florida. Most of them build things.

Fewer of them plan.

At Keentel, we lead with pre-construction because we believe the most valuable thing we can do for a client is reduce the uncertainty and risk of their project — before the construction clock starts running.

A project that's been through rigorous pre-construction planning builds faster, builds cheaper, and produces fewer surprises. That's not a marketing claim. It's what happens when you solve problems on paper instead of in concrete.

We serve commercial, industrial, institutional, and residential clients across Tampa Bay, Orlando, Miami, Jacksonville, Fort Lauderdale, and all of Florida. Whatever your project type, whatever your market, whatever your timeline — pre-construction is where we start.

And it's where your project's success is determined.

faqs.a: It depends on project complexity. Simple commercial renovations may complete pre-construction in 3–4 weeks. Mid-size ground-up commercial projects typically require 6–10 weeks. Complex developments, healthcare facilities, or industrial projects may need 12–20 weeks of thorough pre-construction work. The investment in time is returned many times over in construction phase efficiency.

Pre-construction is typically either included in the GC's overall contract or billed as a separate pre-construction services fee — often 1–3% of estimated construction cost. This fee is the single highest-ROI expenditure in the project. A $30,000 pre-construction investment that prevents a $300,000 construction-phase problem pays for itself ten times over.

faqs.q: What is a constructability review and why does it matter?
faqs.a: A constructability review is the process of evaluating architectural and engineering drawings for real-world buildability — checking whether the design can be executed as drawn, at the specified cost, in the stated timeframe. Issues caught in constructability review are resolved with a red-line markup. The same issues caught during construction are resolved with a change order. The cost difference is dramatic.

faqs.q: What is value engineering in pre-construction?
faqs.a: Value engineering is the process of identifying design alternatives that achieve the same functional outcome at reduced cost. It is not cost-cutting or cheapening the project. It's asking 'is there a way to achieve this goal more efficiently?' The best value engineering happens during design — before specifications are locked and before the design team has to go back and redo work.

faqs.q: Can pre-construction happen in parallel with design?
faqs.a: Yes — and this is actually the ideal model. When the contractor is involved during the design phase, design decisions are informed by cost and constructability input in real time. This is the core principle of Design-Build delivery, but it can also apply in traditional project delivery when the owner chooses to engage the GC during design rather than after.

faqs.q: What happens if we skip pre-construction to save time?
faqs.a: You don't save time. You borrow it — at a very high interest rate. Projects that skip pre-construction consistently experience longer construction phases, higher final costs, more change orders, and more disputes than projects with thorough planning. The time 'saved' by skipping pre-construction is typically repaid three to five times over during construction.
